name: Distributed Systems Fundamentals Interview Prep
description: 20 advanced questions on consistency, consensus, replication, ordering, failure detection, and split-brain behavior in distributed systems.

cards.front: 1. What is partition tolerance, really?
cards.back: It means the system keeps operating, in some form, when the network splits and nodes cannot reliably talk to each other. In practice, every real distributed system must assume partitions happen.

cards.front: 2. What is the difference between consistency models?
cards.back: Consistency models define what a read is allowed to observe after a write. Linearizability is strongest, while eventual consistency allows temporary divergence that later converges.

cards.front: 3. Why are consensus protocols important?
cards.back: They let multiple nodes agree on one ordered history of decisions even when some nodes fail. That agreement is the basis for leader election, replicated logs, and strongly consistent metadata.

cards.front: 4. How do Raft and Paxos fit into system design interviews?
cards.back: They are reference points for understanding how a cluster elects a leader and keeps a consistent log. You usually need the concepts, not the formal proofs.

cards.front: 5. What is quorum, and why does it matter?
cards.back: A quorum is the minimum number of replicas required to read or write safely. By tuning read and write quorums, you can trade availability, latency, and consistency.

cards.front: 6. What causes split-brain?
cards.back: Split-brain happens when two sides of a partition both believe they are the primary and accept conflicting writes. It is a classic reason for fencing tokens and careful leader election.

cards.front: 7. How do you think about replication lag?
cards.back: Replication lag is the time between a write on the primary and the write becoming visible on replicas. It matters because it creates stale reads, failover risk, and correctness edge cases.

cards.front: 8. What is the difference between primary-backup and multi-leader replication?
cards.back: Primary-backup centralizes writes and simplifies conflict handling, while multi-leader improves local write availability but introduces conflict resolution complexity. The choice is usually driven by latency and failure tolerance.

cards.front: 9. Why is clock sync hard in distributed systems?
cards.back: Physical clocks drift, network delays vary, and no system can assume perfectly synchronized time. That is why logical clocks and ordering schemes often matter more than wall-clock timestamps.

cards.front: 10. What is the role of logical clocks?
cards.back: Logical clocks help reason about causality and event ordering when wall-clock time is unreliable. They are useful for conflict resolution, versioning, and detecting concurrent updates.

cards.front: 11. Why is exactly-once processing so hard?
cards.back: A system can usually do at-least-once or at-most-once, but true exactly-once requires coordination across retries, storage, and side effects. The practical answer is usually idempotency plus deduplication.

cards.front: 12. What is idempotency in distributed APIs?
cards.back: An operation is idempotent if repeating it produces the same external result. That property makes retries safe and is essential for unreliable networks.

cards.front: 13. How do you handle duplicate messages or duplicate requests?
cards.back: Use request IDs, deduplication storage, idempotent writes, or a transaction log that records what has already been processed. The goal is to make replay harmless.

cards.front: 14. What is the difference between failure detection and failure recovery?
cards.back: Detection answers whether a node or dependency is likely unhealthy; recovery answers what the system does next. A good design does not confuse a suspicion of failure with proof of failure.

cards.front: 15. Why are retries dangerous in distributed systems?
cards.back: Retries can amplify traffic, duplicate side effects, and turn a partial outage into a total one. They need limits, jitter, and backoff so they help availability instead of destroying it.

cards.front: 16. What is the role of fencing tokens?
cards.back: Fencing tokens ensure that an old or partitioned writer cannot continue mutating state after a newer leader takes over. They are a practical defense against zombie leaders.

cards.front: 17. How do CRDTs differ from traditional conflict resolution?
cards.back: CRDTs are built to converge automatically without coordination, which makes them useful in highly available systems. Traditional conflict resolution often requires explicit application logic after divergence.

cards.front: 18. What is the PACELC trade-off?
cards.back: PACELC says a distributed system trades availability and consistency during partitions, and latency versus consistency when the network is healthy. It is a useful framework for explaining real design choices.

cards.front: 19. Why does ordering matter so much?
cards.back: Many correctness bugs are really ordering bugs: duplicate processing, missed causality, or state applied out of sequence. If the order matters, the architecture must make that guarantee explicit.

cards.front: 20. When is a distributed system too complex for its value?
cards.back: When the business problem is simple enough that the operational and correctness costs outweigh the benefit of distribution. Staff engineers should be willing to keep something single-region, single-writer, or even single-node if that is the right trade-off.

author: Gemini
